newsitem.title: USA: Clinton inaugural to use QVC as fund-raiser.
newsitem.headline: Clinton inaugural to use QVC as fund-raiser.

text.p: Now available, from the television shopping channel that brought cubic zirconia to the nation ... a presidential inaugural.

Organisers of the second inauguration of President Clinton, who has faced scrutiny over aggressive campaign fund raising, said Tuesday they were hoping to raise a few million dollars for the festivities by selling commemorative items through shopping network QVC Inc.

"The sale of commemoratives is a key component of our budget, allowing us to forgo the large loans and contributions that have been used to finance previous inaugurals," the official Presidential Inaugural Committee said.
On sale are bronze, silver and gold presidential medallions, collector plates, postmarked envelopes, automobile license plates and an American eagle pin featuring a "ruby eye."
An inital offering of inaugural items Monday evening "far exceeded" expectations, QVC spokeswoman Ellen Rubin said.
She said the inaugural committee, which approached QVC with the idea, aimed to raise in the "low- to mid-seven figures" through the sales.
"I think that would be a good amount," said inaugural committee spokesman David Seldin.
The total budget for the Jan. 20 inaugural and related activities is $30 million, he said.
The committee has put a $100 maximum limit on contributions and is not accepting loans or in-kind contributions.
QVC also will broadcast coverage of the inaugural beginning on Jan. 18.

Although QVC, a subsidiary of Comcast Corp., made its name selling items such as costume jewelry and housewares, it has recently ventured into high-toned markets with programmes and sales on cultural themes such as last year's Cezanne exhibition at the Philadelphia art museum.

"QVC's track record of bringing big, live events into people's homes and to simultaneously market related quality products is what drove our decision to choose them..." the inaugural committee said, adding that ... "they understand how to provide the proper context to merchandise in a dignified way."
Seldin said the commemorative merchandise also is being sold through a catalogue and two stores in Washington. "It's not fund-raising, it's selling products," he said of the project.
